reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A clinical syndrome of incoordination arising from cerebellar dysfunction, causing a wide-based unsteady gait, limb dysmetria, and impaired balance
Characteristic signs include intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria on finger-nose and heel-shin testing, and scanning dysarthria
Midline (vermis) lesions predominantly affect gait and truncal stability, whereas hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia
Nystagmus and impaired smooth pursuit and saccades commonly accompany cerebellar disease
Cerebellar ataxia is distinguished from sensory ataxia, in which imbalance worsens markedly with eyes closed (positive Romberg) due to proprioceptive loss
Causes are broad, spanning stroke, tumour, demyelination, alcohol and toxins, hereditary and paraneoplastic syndromes, and metabolic disturbance
Acute cerebellar signs, particularly with headache or reduced consciousness, may indicate a cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can cause life-threatening brainstem compression and hydrocephalus
Investigation is guided by tempo of onset, with acute presentations requiring urgent imaging and chronic ones prompting evaluation for hereditary, degenerative, and metabolic causes
reference.pathophysiology: Cerebellar ataxia reflects impaired function of the cerebellum or its afferent and efferent connections, which normally coordinate the timing, force, and accuracy of movement and maintain balance and posture. Damage to the cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, or connecting peduncles disrupts these predictive and error-correcting mechanisms, producing dysmetria, tremor, and incoordination. The underlying pathology may be vascular, inflammatory, neoplastic, toxic, metabolic, degenerative, or genetic.
additionalDifferentials: Sensory ataxia from dorsal column or large-fibre neuropathy disease
Frontal gait disorder and normal pressure hydrocephalus
Weakness or extrapyramidal disorders mimicking incoordination
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain focusing on the posterior fossa to identify structural, vascular, or demyelinating lesions
Blood tests for metabolic, endocrine, nutritional (including vitamin B12 and E), and toxic causes
Paraneoplastic antibody panel and search for underlying malignancy when subacute cerebellar degeneration is suspected
Genetic testing for hereditary ataxias in chronic progressive cases
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when an inflammatory, infective, or paraneoplastic cause is considered
redFlags: Acute cerebellar signs with headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness suggesting cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can cause brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus requiring emergency neurosurgical assessment
Rapidly progressive ataxia suggesting a paraneoplastic, inflammatory, or toxic cause
Associated cranial nerve or long-tract signs indicating brainstem involvement
New ataxia in a patient on potentially toxic drug levels such as anticonvulsants
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause. Some causes, such as drug toxicity, vitamin deficiency, or an inflammatory process, are reversible with treatment, whereas hereditary and neurodegenerative ataxias are typically progressive. Acute cerebellar strokes can be life-threatening but may recover substantially with timely intervention.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish cerebellar from sensory or vestibular ataxia, leading to the wrong workup
Missing a cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can rapidly deteriorate into brainstem compression
Overlooking reversible causes such as drug toxicity, vitamin deficiency, or hypothyroidism
Not pursuing a paraneoplastic cause in subacute progressive cerebellar degeneration
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, with thiamine for alcohol-related disease, vitamin B12 or E replacement for deficiency, and directed treatment of tumour or stroke
Withdraw offending toxins and drugs such as alcohol and anticonvulsant or chemotherapy toxicity
For paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, treat the underlying malignancy and give immunotherapy
Provide balance and gait rehabilitation with physiotherapy and symptomatic management of tremor and incoordination
Involve occupational therapy, speech and language therapy for dysarthria and swallowing, and falls prevention
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for hereditary ataxias
Refer to neurology and escalate urgently for acute cerebellar stroke with mass effect requiring posterior fossa decompression
